Essay #1
About Isabel Marant by Carson Guise
MM/DD/20XX

Note of Intent (NOI)
Fashion itself is at the core of a lot of our daily lives whether we realize it or not. The decisions 
of what to wear and how we want to be perceived go hand and hand. There are so many 
brands to choose from, and with these options comes a lot of clothes that are wasted because 
of changing consumer taste. Textile waste is becoming a leading sustainability issue in the 
world, contributing to 92 million tons per year and being 35% of the plastic in the oceans. 
Currently, consumer demand trends in are shifting towards more sustainable efforts. From 
H&M, to Isabel Marant, to Balmain, we are seeing tremendous amounts of issues in 
sustainability that are affecting everyone in this world, whether they are into fashion or not. 
The ﬁlm “The True Cost” discusses all of the issues surrounding fashion, especially when it 
comes to fast fashion. It highlights where we are currently, where we can move to, and 
showcases stories of those who are trapped by the industry, and those who are trying to 
change it. Powerful spectacles like “The True Cost” provoke us to think about fashion in a 
different way, sparking conversations for brands to do more on their part, one brand at a time. 
By analyzing speciﬁc brands, like Isabel Marant, we can understand where most brands stand, 
where they should improve, and how they can go about doing so.

Ethics & Sustainability Insights
Isabel Marant states that they are pledging to:
●
Move towards more sustainable fashion
●
Employ more sustainable materials in production
●
Achieve a 65% rate of sustainable materials by 2024
On Good On You, Isabel Marant is rated “Not Good Enough”
●
⅕ on Planet
○No evidence they protect biodiversity, reduce / eliminate hazardous chemicals in 
manufacturing, or minimize packaging
●
⅖ on People
○No evidence that they provide ﬁnancial security to supplies (leads to poor working 
conditions and wages), implement DEI practices, or ensure workers are paid living 
wages
●
⅖ on Animals
○No evidence they have a animal welfare policy, trace any animal-derived materials 
to the ﬁrst stage of production, and uses leather, wool, exotic animal fur, and silk 
There is a recent consumer push for the more sustainable production of clothing, but the 
question is which brands are actually sustainable, or performative.

Working Conditions & Workers' Rights
Ensuring that production is ethical is a priority many brands and 
consumers should have. As seen in the ﬁlm “The True Cost,” textile 
production facilities can lead to many issues, such as:
●
Unsafe working conditions that can lead to death
●
Abuse of power from big corporations to push for cheaper 
labor
●
Families torn apart because people cannot make a livable 
wage within these production factories.
While Isabel Marant may not fully disclose where they 
manufacture, this raises concerns of workers rights and what 
goes into making their clothing 
Many brand’s clothes are made in countries where labor is cheap and efficient. Most brands are not transparent about this, such as 
Isabel Marant. On their website does not explicitly say where their collections are made. 
●
Their designs are done in the headquarters of Paris, but they have a supply chain that extends to over 15 countries, 
speciﬁcally Asia, Europe and North Africa
They are very selective with this information, leaving many to believe they participate in actions such as cheap labor that causes 
unfair and unsafe working conditions. 
Where Are Their Main Collections Made?
Why This Is Important

How Brands Contribute To Overconsumption
Brands like H&M and Zara fuel this “need” in consumers minds that they 
need to have the next new style, causing them to purchase. By the time 
they purchase this product, the next new style is already out, meaning 
they have to buy again. This inherently causes overconsumption on the 
mass scale, leading to massive amounts of fashion waste.
When one’s favorite celebrity wears a brand, fans think that they should 
wear the brand, causing them to grab them until the shelfs are 
completely empty. This is what brands like Isabel Marant do with 
celebrity endorsements, like Kate Moss’ recent endorsement of Isabel 
Marant as a face of one of their collections in 2025. 
The higher the demand, the more clothes there are to make, the more 
labor and materials that are required. Overconsumption starts the never 
ending cycle that leads to so much textile waste (92 million tons each 
year) 
Demand-Driven Brands
Celebrity Endorsements
Why Overconsumption Hurts

Environmental Impact from Fashion and Fast Fashion
Most of the time we focus on the environmental impacts that fashion has had on 
us, but rarely about the social effects. As seen in the ﬁlm, stories like Shima Akhter’s 
are reasons change needs to happen. A young mother trying to support her young 
daughter and support her coworkers as a union leader, she is enduring so much to 
get compensated for so little. Consumers’ appetites will never be satisﬁed, and the 
fastest way to satisfy the consumers is with cheap and efficient labor, something 
most companies outsource to countries where labor is cheap yet unethical. Fashion 
isn’t always the glamour we want it to be, and something must change.  
Fashion has massive effects on our world, statistics stat that fashion brands are responsible for:
●
10% of the world’s greenhouse gases
●
35% of the plastic in the ocean and 20% of industrial water pollution
Likewise, the Fashion Weeks are also contributors to the environment, stating that:
●
It causes 241,000 tonnes of CO₂ per year and as much energy as 3,000 years of lighting the Eiffel Tower
New trends of AI in culmination with fast fashion are causing the overproduction of non recyclable clothes, adding to the textile 
waste worldwide. Inherently through their business, Isabel Marant contributes to these statistics, unless they are to change their 
processes. 
How Our World Suﬀers from Fashion
Not Only Does Our Environment Suﬀer, But We Do

In order for sustainability to ensue, brands must look at 
their processes and see where they can improve. For 
materials and production, seeing where they can reduce 
their C02 emissions or water consumption, or how they 
can ensure better working conditions can lead to 
massive innovations worldwide, promoting the global 
economy.
Consumers value a brand that they trust, and when 
things aren’t readily available consumers start to worry, 
especially in a market where sustainability is a big factor 
in the buying process. It is better to be public about 
where your supply chain operates out of rather than hide 
it. The only way we can move to a more ethical fashion 
world is through accountability and action.
While this may seem counterintuitive to a business, one 
way to help reduce waste is by creating less products, or 
rather produce as much that is needed. By underballing 
production numbers, you are saving on production costs 
while assisting the environment. This reinforces the idea 
that fashion is an artform, and rather than being 
available 24/7. 
Pledging to do something and doing something are two 
completely different things. Isabel Marant pledges to do 
a lot in terms of sustainability, but there is a lack of 
evidence to show actions were taken. Being a 
performative brand does not do anything to help your 
brand or our world. Especially when it comes to labor, 
because stories like Shima’s will only become more 
common without change. 
Reevaluate Supply Chains
Promote Scarcity
Become Transparent
All Bite, No Bark
Ethical & Sustainability Recommendations
For All Fashion Brands
For Isabel Marant

Conclusion & Perspectives
Isabel Marant is not the only brand that needs to work on their 
sustainability efforts. We need to see strides from fashion brands all around, 
such as:
●
Shein
●
H&M
●
Zara
This isn’t a one brand can ﬁx it all sort of problem, but rather a case that 
once one shows how it can be done, a better outcome looks more 
attainable. Researchers argue that we are running out of time to change our 
ways before we are “doomed,” making the timing of this change something 
that should be instantaneous. Many fashion brands have taken strides in 
the right direction, such as:
●
People Tree (as mentioned in “The True Cost”)
●
Florania (based in Milan)
While most of this seems like an idealistic view of how fashion brands 
should change, brands must recognize that they can do things, just like 
Isabel Marant, one action at a time to begin to work towards a better 
tomorrow.
